notes: Run plan: eval 3 (wrong-question-detection) runs paired -- with-skill + no-skill baseline -- since Notion vs Obsidian is the one case where a baseline is actually informative (plain Claude will compare the two apps feature-by-feature and never question whether the tool is the problem; Framer catching that while the baseline doesn't is the strongest single example this skill will produce). Evals 1, 2, and 4 run single-agent, with-skill only, per the plan. Eval 2's subject was swapped from a Senegal NGO trip to a generic destination-wedding-during-exam-week scenario -- the repo is public and examples/ is the selling surface; a stranger reading the original learns about the author instead of about the skill. Same shape (personal decision, external event colliding with a school obligation), no autobiography. Watching eval 4 closest: nothing in its prompt says 'quick council', so if the full six-seat panel convenes anyway, the intake gate isn't gating and that's a v1 bug, not a tuning issue. Grading is qualitative per the plan, but mechanical things are asserted: every required output section present, the objection section non-empty, seats capped at 3 sentences (checked via each run's transcript, since the skill's default output shows only the Chair's final block, not individual seats), and whether the consensus-flag mechanism actually fires on any run where all six seats converge.

evals.name: technical-scoping-decision
evals.prompt: My Raspberry Pi life dashboard is a pile of Python scripts at this point and every new feature takes longer to bolt on than the last one. Should I do a full rewrite in something more structured, or just keep patching the Python version?
evals.expected_output: Checks that Builder and Accountant differentiate instead of converging on the same take -- Builder should push toward a small, fast-information move (rewrite one module, not the whole thing) while Accountant should price out the real cost of a full rewrite including ongoing maintenance. A technical decision is the easy case; if the seats sound identical here the panel design has a real problem.
expectations: Output contains every required section from the fixed template: Decision, Confidence, Why (numbered reasons), Strongest objection, Why it loses, What would flip this, Do this first
The Strongest objection section is non-empty and is a real substantive objection, not a restatement of the Decision
Per the transcript, Builder's and Accountant's actual seat contributions are substantively different from each other -- not the same take in different words
Per the transcript, each seat's contribution is 3 sentences or fewer
The full six-seat panel convenes (this decision is not obviously reversible/low-stakes, so the quick-mode gate should NOT fire here)

evals.name: personal-decision-no-business-framing
evals.prompt: A close friend of mine is getting married at a destination wedding, and the date falls right in the middle of exam week senior year. Should I go?
evals.expected_output: The real test of whether the seats stay in register for a personal, emotionally weighted decision instead of lapsing into boardroom language ('stakeholder alignment', 'ROI', 'resourcing'). If any seat sounds like it's talking about a product launch, that's a failure. The Stakeholder seat in particular needs to talk about the friend/parents/teachers as real people with real reactions, not 'stakeholders.'
expectations: Output contains every required section from the fixed template
The Strongest objection section is non-empty
No seat's language reads as boardroom/corporate (no 'stakeholder alignment', 'ROI', 'resourcing', 'deliverables', etc.) anywhere in the transcript or output
The Stakeholder seat's contribution names real people in this scenario (the friend, parents, teachers) rather than generic 'stakeholders'
Per the transcript, each seat's contribution is 3 sentences or fewer

evals.name: wrong-question-detection
evals.prompt: Should I switch from Notion to Obsidian for my notes? I keep hearing Obsidian is better for people who actually stick with note-taking.
evals.expected_output: The Framer should catch that the tool isn't the actual decision -- the real question is whether a note-taking habit exists at all, not which app hosts it. Failure looks like the panel dutifully weighing Notion vs. Obsidian feature-by-feature without anyone naming that the tool swap probably isn't what's broken. Baseline (no skill) is expected to just compare the two apps and never raise this.
evals.run_mode: PAIRED -- with-skill agent + no-skill baseline agent, same prompt
expectations: Output contains every required section from the fixed template
The Strongest objection section is non-empty
Per the transcript, the Framer's contribution explicitly names the real question as the note-taking habit, not the app choice
The Decision or Why section reflects the reframe (addresses the habit question), not just a Notion-vs-Obsidian feature comparison
Per the transcript, each seat's contribution is 3 sentences or fewer
Baseline (no skill) is expected to compare the two apps directly and NOT question whether the tool itself is the problem -- this is the point of the paired run, not a bug in the baseline

evals.name: low-stakes-reversible-autogate
evals.prompt: Should I try switching my main browser from Chrome to Arc for a week to see if I like it?
evals.expected_output: Tests the Step 1 intake gate, not the user typing 'quick council' -- this is a fully reversible, low-stakes decision, and the skill itself should recognize that and drop into quick mode (or something close to it) without being asked. Failure looks like the full six-seat panel plus audit seat producing 800 words for a decision that costs nothing to reverse. THE ONE TO WATCH CLOSEST: if the full panel convenes here, the intake gate isn't gating -- that's a v1 bug, not a tuning issue.
expectations: Quick mode (or something functionally equivalent -- 3 seats, not 6) fires WITHOUT the user typing 'quick council' or 'fast take'
Output is short -- roughly 10 lines, not an 800-word full-panel writeup
Output still contains the required decision-block sections even in quick mode
If the full six-seat panel convenes instead of quick mode, this is flagged explicitly as a v1 bug in the intake gate, not graded as a tuning nitpick

cross_run_checks: On any run where the transcript shows all six full-panel seats converging on the same recommendation, check whether the consensus-flag mechanism (Step 3) actually fired -- explicit statement that unanimous agreement is a flag, and a forced strongest-objection from the Skeptic specifically. This is conditional (only applies if consensus actually happened in a given run), not a universal pass/fail.
